title: The Sunburned Lifeguard
briefing: Kai, 16, worked his first full shift as a junior lifeguard: six hours in the chair, no shirt, forgot the sunscreen. His shoulders looked fine when he left. By bedtime they were bright red and hot to touch. A week later the red was gone and his shoulders were a shade darker than the rest of him.
question: What did the sunlight do, and why did the skin react twice?

clues.title: Six hours of strong sun
clues.text: UV index 8 all afternoon, no shade, no shirt, no sunscreen. His legs, under the chair's shade, were fine.
clues.shows: a large dose of UV energy landing on bare skin

visual.unit: UV units reached the skin, 1 h → 6 h

clues.title: Red hours later
clues.text: Nothing visible at 4 p.m. Bright red and hot by 9 p.m. The redness was only where the sun hit.
clues.shows: a delayed response in exactly the sun-hit skin

clues.title: Peeling on day four
clues.text: The top layer of skin on his shoulders flaked off in thin sheets.
clues.shows: the body shedding cells that were too badly stressed to keep

clues.title: Darker a week later
clues.text: Once the red faded, the shoulders stayed a shade darker than his chest for weeks.
clues.shows: the skin's slow protective response: more melanin

hypotheses.text: The chair's metal frame burned him.
hypotheses.flaw: A hot-metal burn appears instantly and only where metal touched; this appeared hours later across everything the sun reached.

hypotheses.text: UV light damaged his skin cells; the redness is the repair response hours later, peeling clears the worst-hit cells, and extra melanin is the skin preparing for next time.
He is allergic to chlorine from the pool.
hypotheses.flaw: Chlorine touched his whole body, but only the sun-exposed shoulders reacted — and allergies do not leave skin darker afterwards.

hypotheses.text: The heat of the day made his skin red.
hypotheses.flaw: Heat flushes the whole body evenly and fades once you cool down; it does not wait five hours, pick out the sun-hit patches, or cause peeling.

prediction.prompt: Kai sits in strong sun with no protection. As the hours go by — from none up to six — what happens to how red his skin will become?

second.question: If he wears a shirt half the time and sunscreen, what happens to the UV energy reaching his skin?

concepts.label: UV light carries energy
concepts.hint: What in sunlight actually does the damage?

concepts.label: skin cells damaged
concepts.hint: What happened inside the skin before anything was visible?

concepts.label: redness = repair response
concepts.hint: Why did it turn red and hot hours later?

concepts.label: melanin builds protection
concepts.hint: Why did the skin end up darker, and what is that for?

transfer.context: Rosa skis all day on a bright, snowy mountain. That night her cheeks and nose are red and sore even though it was freezing cold.
options: The cold air froze her cheeks.
UV light — made stronger by altitude and reflected by snow — damaged her skin cells, and the redness is the delayed repair response.
transfer.retryHint: Red hours later, only on the parts the light hit — which of Kai's clues matches that?
transfer.explanation: Cold has nothing to do with it: snow reflects UV upward and the thin mountain air filters less of it, so Rosa's face got a big dose. Just like Kai's shoulders, the skin cells were damaged during the day and the repair response — redness and soreness — showed up hours later.

takeaway: Sunlight carries UV energy that damages skin cells. Redness hours later is the repair crew arriving, peeling is the clear-out, and the darker skin afterwards is the body building its own shade for next time.
